strings.name: Moussa Faki Mahamat
strings.role: Former African Union Commission Chairperson and 4P Special Envoy
strings.summary: Moussa Faki Mahamat is a Chadian politician and diplomat who served as prime minister and foreign minister before leading the African Union Commission from 2017 to 2025. His work covered continental integration, peace and security, and institutional reform. In June 2025, after leaving the Commission, he became Special Envoy for the Pact for Prosperity, People and the Planet (4P), promoting discussions on development finance and climate cooperation. This work depends on multilateral institutions and member-state negotiations; collective decisions and policy objectives cannot all be credited as personal achievements.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through November 18, 2026. Current office is supported by official 4P information; recent activity draws on reporting after the October 10–11, 2026 Quy Nhon dialogue. Doctoral enrolment is distinguished from a completed degree, Commission leadership from the rotating AU chairmanship, signatures from implementation, and event invitations from actual attendance.
strings.influence.rationale: He formerly led the African Union Commission and participated in African peace, security and integration affairs, influencing regional multilateral cooperation.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Biltine, Chad, on June 21, 1960. The French CV published by the AU lists a 1986 licence in public law, a 1992 advanced-studies diploma in public law, and enrolment for a public-law doctoral thesis at Paris 13 University. It does not confirm completion of a doctorate or identify the institutions awarding the first two qualifications.
strings.facts.f2.label: Administrative and legal experience
strings.facts.f2.value: He taught law-related subjects at Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville and in N'Djamena, and contributed to drafting Chadian constitutional texts and legal work on Chad–Cameroon oil negotiations. He headed the national sugar company from 1996 to 1999 and the president's civilian office from 1999 to 2002, before holding senior government and diplomatic posts.
strings.highlights.h1.title: The Commission's institutional role
strings.highlights.h1.text: The Commission Chairperson is its chief executive and legal representative, responsible for its administration and reporting to the Executive Council. This differs from the AU chairmanship rotating among member-state heads of state. Faki advocated Agenda 2063, peace and security, and regional integration; these shared objectives do not establish that every conflict or development problem was resolved.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Climate and finance advocacy after leaving office
strings.highlights.h2.text: At the October 2026 Quy Nhon dialogue on climate and transitions in Vietnam, he spoke as 4P Special Envoy about connecting scientific evidence with political action on climate and global financing challenges. VNA's October 11 report records remarks actually delivered. Advocacy alone does not establish that funding was disbursed or a new international agreement concluded.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Becomes 4P Special Envoy
strings.timeline.t1.text: The official 4P profile and Sevilla Declaration confirm his appointment in June 2025 to represent the platform in advancing international financial architecture reform. The platform originated in a 2023 summit and its Secretariat is hosted by the OECD. His envoy role is not that of OECD Secretary-General or a United Nations envoy.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Hands over Commission leadership
strings.timeline.t2.text: At the Addis Ababa handover ceremony, he ended his service as African Union Commission Chairperson and was succeeded by Mahmoud Ali Youssouf. The AU's current leadership information records Faki's tenure as 2017–2025; older pages still calling him chairperson must be read as historical material.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Re-elected Commission Chairperson
strings.timeline.t3.text: He won re-election at the 34th AU summit. The Commission Chairperson serves a four-year term renewable once. The communiqué appeared the next day, so election and publication dates differ; the actual 2025 handover establishes the end of his service.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Advances the continental free-trade agreement process
strings.timeline.t4.text: At the extraordinary summit in Kigali, he addressed the signing of the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement and urged member states to proceed with ratification. The meeting involved separate instruments, including the trade agreement, Kigali Declaration and free movement. Signatories to all instruments cannot be combined as parties to the trade agreement, and signing does not mean trade rules were fully implemented.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Takes charge of the AU Commission
strings.timeline.t5.text: After his January 30 election, he succeeded Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma on March 14. At the handover he outlined priorities including peace and security, youth and women's participation, trade and institutional reform. His objectives and work programme must be assessed separately from subsequent results.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes Chad's foreign minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: He entered the foreign ministry's leadership in April 2008 and served until moving to the AU Commission in 2017. His diplomatic experience included regional peace and security and multilateral cooperation. Historical offices listed in institutional biographies do not mean he remains Chad's foreign minister today.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Heads the Economic, Social and Cultural Council
strings.timeline.t7.text: He chaired Chad's Economic, Social and Cultural Council from February 2007 to April 2008. This was a national institutional role, distinct from his later continental position at the African Union Commission.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Serves as Chad's prime minister
strings.timeline.t8.text: He became prime minister in June 2003 and left in February 2005. IRIN reported on February 4 that he had resigned the previous day amid civil-service strikes over unpaid salaries, but obtained no official reason for his departure. The social context should not be turned into a proven personal motive.
